Your device is humming a note right now. You can't hear it, but your hand is bouncing it straight back, and that echo is what turns these pages. So what's this secret note?

It buzzes 19,000 times a second. Kids can just about catch it, most grown-ups lost it years ago, and your dog hears it loud and clear. Silent to you, it flies out, hits everything in the room and comes back.
Walls, the table, your coffee mug: they all send the note back exactly as it left. Pretty boring, because they sit still. Your hand doesn't, and that's where the siren trick comes in.

Move your hand closer and its echo comes back a touch higher. Pull away and it drops. It's the same trick that bends an ambulance siren as it races past. Higher means toward, lower means away. The bend is tiny, though.

A quick flick of your hand bends the note by about half a percent, far too little for you to notice. Your device checks 23 times a second and only cares which way it bent: up means next, down means back. Clever, but hardly new.

Bats hunt in the dark this way, shouting and reading the echoes. Your device just learned the trick, with no camera, no internet and nothing saved, on the same Kotlin code for phones, laptops and browsers.
A bat finds its way by shouting and listening for the echo. As it closes in on a moth, the shouts speed up to 200 a second. Some are louder than a rock concert, but far too high for us to hear.
A dolphin clicks through the fatty bump on its forehead and hears the echo through its lower jaw. By sound alone, it can tell a hollow ball from a solid one.
Some tiger moths click back at a hunting bat. The clicks jam its sonar, so the bat misses. A whole chase, start to finish, in sounds we will never hear.
That heart-shaped face funnels sound to its ears, and one ear sits higher than the other, so it hears up and down as well as left and right. That's how a barn owl catches a mouse in total darkness.
Dogs hear up to about 45,000 vibrations a second, more than twice what we can, so Wave's note is easy for them. If yours tilts its head at your device, now you know why.
A cat hears past 60,000 vibrations a second, even higher than a dog. Mice squeak up there, out of our range, and each ear swivels on its own to pin down exactly where the squeak came from.
Elephants rumble too low for us to hear, and the sound carries for kilometres. Some of it travels through the ground, and they pick it up with their feet.
